source_read: PDF, Addiction 104: 1085-1099 (all 15 pages): body pp. 1085-1094 read in full; reference list checked for refs 29, 32, 35, 37, 40, 43-60, 65, 71, 76, 78, 104, 105, 107, 112, 123 and 129-133, and searched for the authors' own papers; Table 1 (rotated) and the concentration units on pp. 1087, 1088 and 1091 checked on rendered pages.

key_findings.note: Table 1 read on the rendered p. 1087: half-lives 9.1 (intravenous), 12 (smoked), 9.1 with range 3-17 (oral) and 11 (intranasal), units of Cmax printed as µg/l.

The review says 'emergency department admissions'; the cited DAWN report (ref. 43) is titled as estimates of emergency-department visits, so 'visits' is fair. Refs 29 and 44-51 checked: by their titles, case reports and small case series, the earliest Jordan and Hampson (1960).

By citation: the rhabdomyolysis figure (up to 14%) rests on the treatment trial alone (ref. 54, Richards et al., 1997); the agitation, suicidal-ideation and psychosis figures on refs 52, 54 and 55; the presenting features and seizure figure on refs 52-54, which include ref. 53.
Refs 56-60 checked. Ref. 57 is titled 'Death in amphetamine users: causes and rates'; whether it is a review cannot be told from this PDF, so the card's 'review' is unverified.

Units checked on the rendered p. 1091, where these values are printed: µg/l throughout. The card's note cites only pp. 1087-1088. The card's analysis field calls them blood concentrations; the review says plasma.
Accurate to the review's text, but the review's own sourcing is weaker than its wording: see missed (stroke 'population studies'; the 3.7-fold figure comes from one study, ref. 76).

key_findings.correction: The paragraph also cites one study (ref. 105, Volkow et al., 2001) both for psychomotor dysfunction consistent with Parkinson's disease and for Parkinson-like disturbances in people whose dopaminergic damage was in the Parkinson range, and two studies (refs 107 and 123) that found no such deficits. The case therefore rests on the case-control study (ref. 133, Garwood et al., 2006), the transporter-threshold and age-decline argument, and ref. 105, with two contrary studies noted.

reporting_issues.note: Checked on the rendered p. 1087: '6 ± 11' carries footnote b (geometric mean) and the intranasal '11 ± 1 hours' carries footnote a.
Table 1 gives 169 ± 8 minutes for the intranasal Tmax (ref. 32); the text gives 4 hours (ref. 35).

More exactly, the heart-rate row names beta-adrenoceptors and the blood-pressure row alpha-adrenoceptors, so the blood-pressure entry is a near-copy with the receptor changed. The heart-rate row itself has a word missing ('Amphetamine increased and heart rate').
Reference list checked: 52 Gray et al. 2007, 53 Derlet et al. 1990, 54 Richards et al. 1997, 55 Derlet et al. 1989.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high agreed: the worst domain (appraisal of cited studies) is high, and the overall may not be milder. Instrument none-applicable with the editors' narrative-review checklist fits the design.

risk_of_bias_domains.note: The mislabelled stroke sources (see missed) are a further example.

risk_of_bias_domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
risk_of_bias_domains.note: Reference list searched: no paper by Cruickshank or Dyer among the 183 references.

risk_of_bias_domains.domain: Balance of evidence on adverse effects (descriptions of severe cases against how often harms occur)

interpretation_gap.note: Minor agreed for the review as a whole: the pharmacokinetic and acute-effect summaries follow their sources. The largest gap is the abstract's Parkinson's disease sentence (p. 1085) against the thin support on p. 1093; if this review is cited for a Parkinson's claim, the gap for that claim is substantial.

missed: Stroke 'population studies' (p. 1091, Cardiovascular complications, 3rd paragraph): the two references cited are ref. 50, a series of four cases (Perez et al., 1999), and ref. 78, a population-based study of hospitalized young adults with amphetamine or cocaine diagnoses (Westover et al., 2007). Only one is a population study, and its exposure is not methamphetamine-specific; the 3.7-fold cardiomyopathy figure comes from a single study in young patients (ref. 76, Yeo et al., 2007).

Fatal-overdose statement (p. 1091, 4th paragraph of the overdose section): the report of a fatal overdose after a single intravenous dose rests on one case report (ref. 29, Ago et al., 2006), whose title describes a death nine days after the injection. It cannot be read as describing typical fatal exposures.

The abstract states as fact the amounts typically used illicitly, while the body notes that the self-reports behind them have not been substantiated objectively (p. 1088), adding only that forensic plasma levels are consistent with them.

Card wording: the exposure field says 'several' of the high-dose study's participants had previous psychosis; the review says only that their previous histories of psychosis should be considered (p. 1088), without a number.
